content: 1. Fatty Acids: Fatty acids are a type of lipid that play a crucial role in energy storage, cell membrane structure, and signaling pathways in the body. 2. Fiber: Fiber is a carbohydrate that cannot be digested by the human body. It passes through the digestive system without being absorbed. Soluble fiber absorbs water, while insoluble fiber absorbs much less. 3. Fluorescein Angiography: This is a diagnostic procedure used to visualize the blood flow in the vessels of the eye. It involves injecting a fluorescent dye into the bloodstream and tracking its progress through the eye's blood vessels. 4. Food Exchange: Refer to Exchange Lists for more information. 5. Foot Care: Proper foot care involves taking specific measures to prevent foot problems such as sores, cuts, bunions, and calluses. This includes daily inspection of the feet, toes, and toenails, as well as wearing well-fitting shoes and socks. Individuals with diabetes must be particularly vigilant due to potential nerve damage and reduced blood flow, which can decrease sensation in the feet. This may delay the detection of injuries and impair healing. 6. Fractional Urine: Fractional urine refers to urine collected over specific time intervals during a 24-hour period, such as from breakfast to lunch, lunch to dinner, dinner to bedtime, and bedtime to waking. It is also known as block urine. 7. Fructose: Fructose is a simple sugar commonly found in fruits. It does not directly participate in the glucose metabolism control system but follows a somewhat parallel metabolic pathway to glucose. 8. Fundus of the Eye: The fundus is the central portion of the retina, located at the back or deepest part of the eye. 9. Funduscopy: Funduscopy is a diagnostic test used to examine the back of the eye to assess for damage to the blood vessels supplying the retina. This is performed using an ophthalmoscope or a specialized camera that captures images of the retina, often with dilated pupils, for future comparison. 10. Galactose: Galactose is a simple sugar that does not participate in the glucose metabolism control system. It is one of the two components of lactose, the sugar found in milk. 11. Gangrene: Gangrene is an infection of dead body tissue, most commonly caused by a loss of blood flow. It frequently affects the legs and feet. 12. Gastroparesis: Gastroparesis is a condition resulting from nerve damage that affects the stomach and intestines. It impairs the normal digestion and movement of food, leading to symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, and bloating. This condition often complicates diabetes management. (See also: Autonomic Neuropathy.) 13. Gene: A gene is a unit of heredity. For example, eye color is determined by specific genes, with brown eye genes being dominant over blue eye genes. Genes are segments of DNA and are often regulated by other genes. In glucose absorption, the gene responsible for opening glucose ports in the cell wall is typically inhibited by the product of another gene. This process is well understood and conserved across species, including nematode worms, fish, mice, pigs, cows, and humans. 14. Genetic: See also Heredity. 15. Gestation: Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is a type of diabetes that occurs during pregnancy, typically in the later stages. It is characterized by elevated blood glucose levels, which usually return to normal after delivery in about 95% of cases. Proper medical management is essential to prevent complications for both the mother and the child. When treated appropriately, there are typically no lasting effects. 16. Gingivitis: Gingivitis is a chronic, low-grade infection of the gums. 17. Gland: A gland is an organ that produces and releases substances such as hormones or other secretions. 18. Glaucoma: Glaucoma is a condition characterized by increased internal pressure within the eye, often due to reduced outflow of fluid. Prolonged and elevated pressure can lead to vision loss and, in severe cases, blindness. 19. Gliclazide: Gliclazide is an oral medication used to lower blood glucose levels. It is prescribed for certain individuals with non-insulin-dependent diabetes. It belongs to the sulfonylurea class of drugs. (Brand name: Diamicron™) 20. Glimepiride: Glimepiride is an oral medication used to reduce blood glucose levels. It is prescribed for some individuals with non-insulin-dependent diabetes. It is part of the sulfonylurea drug class. (Brand name: Amaryl™) 21. Glipizide: Glipizide is an oral medication used to lower blood glucose levels. It is prescribed for certain individuals with non-insulin-dependent diabetes. It belongs to the sulfonylurea class of drugs. (Brand name: Glucotrol™) 22. Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR): GFR is a measure of the kidneys' ability to filter and remove waste products from the blood. 23. Glomeruli: Glomeruli are networks of tiny blood vessels in the kidneys where blood filtration occurs, and waste products are removed. 24. Glucagon: Glucagon is a hormone that raises blood glucose levels by stimulating the liver to release stored glucose. 25. Glucose: Glucose is a simple sugar and the primary carbohydrate fuel in food. 26. Glucose Tolerance Test: This test is used to diagnose diabetes. It is typically conducted in the morning after fasting. A blood sample is taken, followed by the consumption of a glucose-containing liquid. Additional blood samples are collected at regular intervals to assess how the body processes glucose over time. The number and timing of samples may vary depending on the laboratory. 27. Glyburide (also called Glibenclamide): Glyburide is an oral medication used to lower blood glucose levels. It is prescribed for some individuals with non-insulin-dependent diabetes. It belongs to the sulfonylurea class of drugs. (Brand names: Diabeta™, Glynase™, Micronase™, Euglucon™) 28. Glycemic Index: The glycemic index measures the effect of different foods on blood glucose levels over time. Some foods, such as cooked carrots, can raise blood glucose levels faster than pure glucose. However, foods are rarely consumed in isolation, and the presence of other foods can alter the results. A more comprehensive measure is glycemic density, which combines the glycemic index with the carbohydrate content of the food. 29. Glycogen: Glycogen is a storage form of glucose composed of multiple glucose molecules. It is sometimes referred to as animal starch. Glycogen is stored in the liver and muscle cells and can be converted back into glucose when needed. Liver glycogen can be released into the bloodstream to maintain blood glucose levels. 30. Glycogenesis: Glycogenesis is the process of forming glycogen from glucose. This process is regulated by insulin. (See also: Glycogen.) 31. Glycosuria: Glycosuria refers to the presence of glucose in the urine.
